t.5.49.1: Having observed that mighty being, the courageous best of monkeys, unperturbed, spoke to the ten-faced one words full of meaning.
t.5.49.2: O lord of the Rākṣasas, I have come here to your abode at the command of Sugrīva. The lord of the monkeys, your brother, has asked after your welfare.
t.5.49.3: Hear the message of your brother, the great-souled Sugrīva, words grounded in dharma and artha, fitting both in this world and the next.
t.5.49.4: There was a king named Daśaratha, possessed of chariots, elephants and horses, a kinsman to the world like a father, his splendour equal to that of the lord of the gods.
t.5.49.5: His eldest son, the mighty-armed lord who brought him joy, departed at his father's command and entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
t.5.49.6: One named Rāma, of great splendor, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and also with his wife Sītā, took refuge in the righteous path.
t.5.49.7: His wife Sītā, devoted to her husband, was lost in the forest; she is the daughter of the great-souled Janaka, king of Videha.
t.5.49.8: That prince, searching for that queen together with his younger brother, reached Ṛśyamūka and became allied with Sugrīva.
t.5.49.10: Then that prince, having slain Vālin in battle, established Sugrīva in the kingdom as lord of the hosts of monkeys and bears.
t.5.49.9: He promised him the search for Sītā, and Rāma, for his part, bestowed upon Sugrīva the kingdom of the monkeys.
t.5.49.11: That Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys and true to his promise, intent on the search for Sītā, dispatched monkeys to all the directions.
t.5.49.12: Hundreds, thousands and myriads of monkeys are searching for her in all the directions, below on the earth and above in the sky.
t.5.49.13: Some there were equal to Vainateya, some like the wind, those mighty monkey heroes, swift, their course unimpeded.
t.5.49.14: I, however, am named Hanumān, the true-born son of Māruta. For the sake of Sītā, having swiftly leapt across the ocean stretching a hundred yojanas, I have come here wishing to see her.
t.5.49.15: Therefore, O greatly wise one, you who have perceived the true meaning of dharma and have gained this prosperity through austerity, should not lay hold of the wives of others.
t.5.49.16: For wise ones such as you do not attach themselves to deeds that are opposed to dharma, that are fraught with many dangers, and that destroy one at the very root.
t.5.49.18: And, O king, there could not be found anyone in the three worlds who, having done wrong to Rāghava, would obtain happiness.
t.5.49.17: And who, even among the gods and asuras, is able to stand before the arrows bidden to Lakṣmaṇa, arrows that follow upon the wrath of Rāma?
t.5.49.19: Regard as true this counsel, which is beneficial for all three times, righteous and conducive to your welfare: let Jānakī be given back to the lord of men.
t.5.49.20: For this queen has been seen by me, and what is hard to attain here has been attained. As for the further task that remains, Rāghava is the cause in that.
t.5.49.21: I have seen this Sītā, so utterly given over to grief, whom you have seized without recognizing that she is like a five-headed she-serpent.
t.5.49.22: She cannot be digested even by the immortals together with the asuras, by any strength, just as food heavily mixed with poison, once eaten, cannot be digested.
t.5.49.23: This store of righteousness that you have won through the burning heat of austerities is the very support of your own self and life, and it is not right to destroy it.
t.5.49.24: As for the invulnerability to the gods together with the asuras that you see as your own through your austerities, even in that there is this weighty reason to consider.
t.5.49.25: For this Sugrīva is neither a Deva nor an Asura, nor a human; he is neither a Rākṣasa nor a Gandharva, neither a Yakṣa nor a serpent.
t.5.49.26: Rāghava is a man, O king, and Sugrīva is the lord of the monkeys; therefore, O king, how will you secure the protection of your life?
t.5.49.28: The fruit of your righteousness has so far been obtained by you; of this there is no doubt. Very soon you will obtain the fruit of this unrighteousness as well.
t.5.49.27: The fruit of dharma does not come mixed with the fruit of adharma; one is followed only by the fruit of what one has done, and dharma is the destroyer of adharma.
t.5.49.29: Having understood the slaughter at Janasthāna, and having understood likewise the slaying of Vālin and the friendship of Rāma and Sugrīva, understand what is good for yourself.
t.5.49.30: Indeed, even I alone am capable of destroying Laṅkā with its horses, chariots and elephants; but this is his firm resolve.
t.5.49.31: For Rāma has vowed, in the presence of the hosts of monkeys and bears, the destruction of those enemies by whom Sītā has been violated.
t.5.49.32: For even Puraṃdara himself, if he wronged Rāma, would find no happiness, nor would anyone else; how much less, then, a person such as you!
t.5.49.33: She whom you know as Sītā, she who now stands in your power, know her to be Kālarātri, the destroyer of all Laṅkā.
t.5.49.34: Enough, then, of this noose of Death in bodily form, Sītā, which you yourself have hung upon your own shoulder; let what is good for yourself be considered.
t.5.49.35: Behold this city with its towers and gateways being consumed by fire, burnt by the splendour of Sītā and oppressed by the wrath of Rāma.
t.5.49.36: Having heard the unwelcome words, full of excellence, of the monkey who spoke without faintheartedness, the matchless Daśānana, his eyes rolling with rage, ordered the slaying of that great monkey.
